svg.aria-label: BGP on Azure gateways: the SKU and type prerequisites, the reserved and usable ASN ranges including the default that is also forbidden, the peer addressing rules, what Azure advertises and accepts, and the fixed timers and prefix ceiling
svg.title: Enabling BGP on an Azure gateway hands four decisions to Azure: the ASN space you may occupy, which prefixes it will accept, how fast a dead peer is noticed, and how many routes exist before the session is dropped
svg.text: A checkbox for dynamic routing — and four decisions you hand to Azure
PREREQUISITES
Supported on every VPN Gateway SKU EXCEPT Basic · route-based gateways ONLY, never policy-based.
On ExpressRoute, BGP is not optional — it is the only way to advertise on-premises routes.
THE ASN RULES
Azure reserves
12076 is the ExpressRoute ASN — reserved globally, not just on circuits.
IANA reserves
Usable private
65515 is BOTH Azure’s default gateway ASN — assigned whether BGP is on or not — AND an ASN you
are forbidden to use on-premises. Mirroring the number on the gateway blade is a refused config.
65516 appears in NEITHER list
not reserved, not inside either usable range. The two lists
are not complements — trust the usable ranges, not “not reserved”.
On-prem and Azure must use DIFFERENT ASNs. 4-byte ASNs work, but only via PowerShell, CLI or SDK — not the portal.
PEER ADDRESSING
Azure side
allocated automatically from the GatewaySubnet range — ONE address for
active-standby, TWO for active-active. Read it from bgpPeeringAddress.
Your side
must NOT be the device’s public IP, nor from the gateway’s VNet space.
A loopback is the right answer. APIPA (169.254.x.x) needs Azure APIPA addresses too.
The Address space field does TWO jobs once BGP is on. Omit the peer /32 — Azure adds it internally,
a documented reversal. Anything ELSE there becomes a STATIC route alongside the BGP ones.
Azure initiates the peering, from its private address. Add a host route for it pointing down the IPsec tunnel.
WHAT AZURE ADVERTISES, AND WHAT IT WILL ACCEPT
It advertises
your VNet prefixes · each connected local network gateway’s prefixes · routes
learned from other BGP sessions — but NEVER the default route, and never
routes overlapping a virtual network prefix.
Whether YOU may advertise your own VNet prefix depends on GATEWAY TRANSIT:
transit ON
Azure BLOCKS or FILTERS it. A /16 VNet lets you advertise /8 — but not /16, and
not /24 either. Only a supernet works; more-specific is refused too.
transit OFF
the gateway never learns peered prefixes, so exact advertisement becomes possible.
Prefix ceiling: 4,000 — and exceeding it DROPS THE SESSION, not the surplus.
Same number and same failure mode as ExpressRoute private peering. So the count is an availability parameter, not a capacity one.
Advertising 0.0.0.0/0 force-tunnels all egress AND stops VMs accepting inbound internet traffic such as RDP or SSH.
OPERATIONAL FACTS
Timers are FIXED
keepalive 60s, hold 180s — a 3:1 ratio, not configurable.
Only your side can change, so a mismatch is yours to avoid. 180s is also the
FLOOR on failure detection — the number to put beside any failover claim.
No BFD on VPN
unsupported for site-to-site — in contrast to ExpressRoute private peerings,
where BFD is configured by DEFAULT. Sub-second on a circuit; three minutes on a tunnel.
Transit routing
works, but needs BGP on EVERY intermediate connection — one non-BGP hop
breaks the chain. Default routes are never propagated onward, which bounds the
blast radius of an accidental 0.0.0.0/0 to the gateway that learned it.
BGP and non-BGP connections can share one gateway. Redundant tunnels to one site need BGP on both and each counts against the tunnel quota.
Multiple tunnels between two virtual networks require at least one gateway in active-active. BGP works in ExpressRoute and VPN coexistence.
Route propagation must never be disabled on GatewaySubnet, and BGP-learned prefixes land in the route table of EVERY subnet in the virtual network.
